teaser: Eleven men, one rope, one ship. And each face is a different story.
review_notes:
Dimensions 131.5 x 281 cm.
Repin first saw haulers on the Neva in 1868-69; Volga trips from 1870; painting finished 1873.
Lead hauler Kanin, a defrocked priest; the boy called Larka; the bent man with headband a former sailor (Ilka): names from Repin's memoirs.
Bought by Grand Duke Vladimir Alexandrovich (3,000 rubles is often cited, not stated in lesson); said to have hung in his billiard room.
Shown at the Vienna World's Fair of 1873.
Dostoevsky's praise (A Writer's Diary, 1873) paraphrased, not quoted.
Pouch in the old man's hands read as a tobacco pouch.
Small vessel with smoke on the horizon read as a steam tug.
Flag on the mast: often said to be a Russian tricolor flown upside down; not stated in lesson.
Villagers' fear that posing meant selling one's soul (Repin's memoirs).
Women in hauling gangs and seasonal lump payment to the team (artel).
Friend who talked Repin out of the rich/poor contrast: Fyodor Vasilyev.
Reuse of the image on stamps and in cartoons.

lesson.text: How do you get a loaded cargo ship up a river when there is no wind and no engine? For centuries, along the Volga in Russia, the answer was: you hire men, strap them into leather harnesses, and have them walk the bank, dragging the boat behind them. They were called burlaki. They worked from the spring thaw until the autumn frosts.

Ilya Repin was a 24-year-old art student in Saint Petersburg when he first saw such a gang, on a sunny day out by the river Neva. Elegant picnickers in summer clothes on one side, and coming toward them, a string of ragged men pulling like oxen. The contrast stayed with him.

His first idea was to paint exactly that contrast, rich against poor. A friend talked him out of it: too obvious, too much like a sermon. So Repin went to the Volga in the summer of 1870, lived in a village for months, and got to know the haulers one by one.
The villagers were suspicious of the young men with sketchbooks. Some believed that having your likeness drawn meant selling your soul, and Repin had trouble persuading anyone to pose.
What he brought back was a group portrait. There are eleven men here, and Repin refuses to let them become a crowd. Each has an age, a temper, a way of leaning into the strap.

lesson.title: Four of the eleven
lesson.text: Start at the front of the line and move back.

spots.title: Kanin
spots.text: The leader, with a rag tied around his head and a steady, sad gaze aimed at you. Repin said he was a former priest and admired him as a kind of philosopher in rags.

spots.title: The fighter
spots.text: Bent lower than anyone, bare shoulder through a torn shirt, he glares out from under his brows. Of the whole gang, he looks the least resigned.

spots.title: The pipe
spots.text: A tall man stands almost straight, pipe in his teeth, hat pushed back. He lets the others do the pulling. Every team has one.

spots.title: The last man
spots.text: At the back, a head hanging so low that the face disappears. He is nearly done. Repin ends the line with exhaustion.

lesson.text: Did you feel the range? Stubbornness, laziness, anger, collapse. Now go to the middle of the line, because one figure breaks the pattern. He is the brightest patch of color in the painting, and the only body that is not bowed.
See how the composition makes him stand out.

lines.label: The bent backs
lines.text: The heads form one low, sagging chain of browns and grays, each man tilted forward into the strap.

lines.label: The boy
lines.text: A teenager in a faded pink shirt stands upright and tugs at the strap on his chest as if it does not fit. He is new to this. He has not learned to give in yet.

lines.label: Toward the ship
lines.text: The line of men runs back along the bank, shrinking toward the barge. They seem to walk out of the picture toward you, with the ship still far behind.

lesson.text: Repin's gang moves from old to young and from broken to defiant. The boy at the center is the question the painting asks: will he end up like the men around him?

The size helps. The canvas is 2.8 meters wide (over 9 feet) and long like a movie screen, so in the museum the men pass in front of you nearly life-size. Repin put the viewpoint low, near the sand. They tower against a huge, empty sky.
A hauling gang could include women, and whole teams were often hired by the season for a single lump payment, shared out at the end if all went well.

And the sunshine. Repin could have chosen rain and mud. He chose a glorious hot day, golden sand, pale blue water. The beauty of the river makes the harness harder to look at. There is one more detail out on the water that changes the meaning of the whole scene.
Something on this river makes these men unnecessary. Can you find it?

spots.title: A steamboat
spots.text: Far off, a tiny vessel trails a ribbon of smoke. Steam tugs were already working the Volga. The machine that could free these men exists, and they are still in harness.

lesson.text: So this is a scene about a way of life that should already be over. By the 1870s steam power was pushing human towing off the big rivers, but men were cheap, and owners used them where they could. Repin never says so in words. He leaves a puff of smoke on the horizon.
The buyer was no rebel. Grand Duke Vladimir, a son of the tsar, bought the painting and is said to have hung it in his billiard room, where he liked to explain the characters to his guests.

spots.title: The giant
spots.text: First on the left, a mop of curly hair and a broad, weathered face. He pulls beside Kanin with his arms hanging loose.

spots.title: Busy hands
spots.text: An old man with a gray beard looks down at a small pouch in his fingers, probably tobacco. He manages a private moment while walking in harness.

spots.title: Looking back
spots.text: A tall figure in a cap turns his head away, toward the barge or the far bank. Of all eleven, his thoughts are furthest from here.

spots.title: On deck
spots.text: Small figures stand on the barge, one in a red shirt at the tiller. They ride. The eleven walk.

spots.title: The flag
spots.text: A striped pennant flutters at the top of the mast. So there is a breeze, though not one that will fill a sail and spare the men.

spots.title: The basket
spots.text: A broken wicker basket half buried in the sand. Worn out and thrown away on the same bank the men are walking.

spots.title: A white sail
spots.text: At the far left another boat glides by under sail, with no one straining at all.

lesson.text: Shown in Saint Petersburg and then at the Vienna World's Fair in 1873, the picture made Repin famous before he turned thirty. The novelist Fyodor Dostoevsky praised it for a precise reason: the haulers do not beg for pity. They are simply themselves, and that, he felt, moves you more than any accusation.

Not everyone agreed. Conservative voices called it an insult to art and to Russia. Younger painters took it as permission. Repin joined the Wanderers, a group of artists who left the official academy system to tour exhibitions around the country, showing Russians their own lives.

The haulers disappeared from the Volga within a couple of generations. The painting stayed, and kept being reused: on stamps, in schoolbooks, in cartoons whenever someone wanted an image of people dragging a weight that is not theirs. Eleven strangers from one summer became the faces of a whole country.

quiz.question: What job did the burlaki do?
options: They towed ships upriver by walking the bank in harness
quiz.explanation: They dragged boats against the current with straps across their chests.

quiz.question: Which figure stands upright in the middle of the line?
options: A boy in a pink shirt
The old man with a pouch
quiz.explanation: The teenager tugs at his strap and has not yet learned to bow.

quiz.question: What small detail shows that this labor was already outdated?
quiz.explanation: A distant steam vessel shows machines could already do the work.

quiz.question: Why did Repin drop his first idea of haulers next to elegant picnickers?
options: A friend found it too obvious, like a sermon
quiz.explanation: He was persuaded that the plain contrast of rich and poor preached too much.

quiz.question: Who bought the painting?
options: Grand Duke Vladimir, a son of the tsar
quiz.explanation: The grand duke bought it and is said to have hung it in his billiard room.

quiz.question: What did Dostoevsky admire in the picture?
options: That the haulers do not beg for pity
quiz.explanation: He felt the men's simple presence moved viewers more than an accusation would.

facts.text: Repin painted the haulers under a dark, rainy sky.
facts.explanation: He chose a bright hot day, which makes the harness harder to look at.

facts.text: There are eleven haulers, and Repin gave each one a distinct character.
facts.explanation: He spent months on the Volga getting to know the men individually.

facts.text: Repin was already an old, established master when he painted this.
facts.explanation: He was in his twenties and the picture made him famous before thirty.
